{{Short description|Statistical property of collections of time series data}}

In [[econometrics]], '''cointegration''' is a [[statistical]] property that describes a long-run equilibrium relationship among two or more [[time series]] variables, even if the individual series are [[non-stationary]] (i.e., they contain stochastic trends). In such cases, the variables may drift in the short run, but their linear combination is stationary, implying that they move together over time and remain bound by a stable equilibrium.

More formally, if several time series are individually [[Order of integration|integrated of order]] ''d'' (meaning they require ''d'' [[Differencing|differences]] to become stationary) but a [[linear combination]] of them is integrated of a lower order, then those time series are said to be cointegrated. That is, if (''X'',''Y'',''Z'') are each integrated of order ''d'', and there exist coefficients ''a'',''b'',''c'' such that {{math|''aX''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''bY''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''cZ''}} is integrated of order less than d, then ''X'', ''Y'', and ''Z'' are cointegrated.  

Cointegration is a crucial concept in time series analysis, particularly when dealing with variables that exhibit trends, such as [[Macroeconomics|macroeconomic]] data. In an influential paper,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nelson |first1=C.R |last2=Plosser |first2=C.I |year=1982 |title=Trends and random walks in macroeconomic time series |journal=[[Journal of Monetary Economics]] |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=139–162 |doi=10.1016/0304-3932(82)90012-5}}</ref> Charles Nelson and [[Charles Plosser]] (1982) provided statistical evidence that many US macroeconomic time series (like GNP, wages, employment, etc.) have stochastic trends.

==Introduction==
If two or more series are individually  [[Order of integration|integrated]] (in the time series sense) but some [[linear combination]] of them has a lower [[order of integration]], then the series are said to be cointegrated. A common example is where the individual series are first-order integrated ({{tmath|I(1)}}) but some (cointegrating) vector of coefficients exists to form a [[Stationary process|stationary]] linear combination of them. 

===History===
The first to introduce and analyse the concept of spurious—or nonsense—regression was [[Udny Yule]] in 1926.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Yule |first=U. |s2cid=126346450 |year=1926 |title= Why do we sometimes get nonsense-correlations between time series? - A study in sampling and the nature of time series | journal=[[Journal of the Royal Statistical Society]] |volume=89 |issue=1 |pages=11–63 |doi=10.2307/2341482 |jstor=2341482 }}</ref>
Before the 1980s, many economists used [[linear regression]]s on non-stationary time series data, which Nobel laureate [[Clive Granger]] and [[Paul Newbold]] showed to be a dangerous approach that could produce [[spurious correlation]],<ref name="GrangerNewbold">{{cite journal |last1=Granger |first1=C. |last2=Newbold |first2=P. |year=1974 |title=Spurious Regressions in Econometrics |journal=[[Journal of Econometrics]] |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=111–120 |doi=10.1016/0304-4076(74)90034-7 |citeseerx=10.1.1.353.2946 }}</ref> since standard detrending techniques can result in data that are still non-stationary.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Clive |last=Granger |year=1981 |title=Some Properties of Time Series Data and Their Use in Econometric Model Specification |journal=[[Journal of Econometrics]] |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=121–130 |doi=10.1016/0304-4076(81)90079-8 }}</ref> Granger's 1987 paper with [[Robert Engle]] formalized the cointegrating vector approach, and coined the term.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Engle |first1=Robert F. |last2=Granger |first2=Clive W. J. |year=1987 |title=Co-integration and error correction: Representation, estimation and testing |journal=[[Econometrica]] |volume=55 |issue=2 |pages=251–276 |jstor=1913236 |doi=10.2307/1913236 |url=http://pe.cemi.rssi.ru/pe_2015_3_106-135.pdf }}</ref>

For integrated {{tmath|I(1)}} processes, Granger and Newbold showed that de-trending does not work to eliminate the problem of spurious correlation, and that the superior alternative is to check for co-integration. Two series with {{tmath|I(1)}} trends can be co-integrated only if there is a genuine relationship between the two. Thus the standard current methodology for time series regressions is to check all-time series involved for integration. If there are {{tmath|I(1)}} series on both sides of the regression relationship, then it is possible for regressions to give misleading results.

The possible presence of cointegration must be taken into account when choosing a technique to test hypotheses concerning the relationship between two variables having [[unit root]]s (i.e. integrated of at least order one).<ref name="GrangerNewbold" /> The usual procedure for testing hypotheses concerning the relationship between non-stationary variables was to run [[ordinary least squares]] (OLS) regressions on data which had been differenced. This method is biased if the non-stationary variables are cointegrated.

For example, regressing the consumption series for any country (e.g. Fiji) against the GNP for a randomly selected dissimilar country (e.g. Afghanistan) might give a high [[R-squared]] relationship (suggesting high explanatory power on Fiji's consumption from Afghanistan's [[GNP]]). This is called [[Spurious correlation|spurious regression]]: two integrated {{tmath|I(1)}} series which are not directly causally related may nonetheless show a significant correlation.

==Tests==
The six main methods for testing for cointegration are:

===Engle–Granger two-step method===
{{see also|Error correction model#Engle and Granger 2-step approach}}
If <math>x_t</math> and <math>y_t</math> both have [[order of integration]] ''d''=1 and are cointegrated, then a linear combination of them must be stationary for some value of <math>\beta</math> and <math>u_t</math> .  In other words:

: <math>
y_t - \beta x_t = u_t \,
</math>

where <math>u_t</math> is stationary.

If <math>\beta</math> is known, we can test <math>u_t</math> for stationarity with an [[augmented Dickey–Fuller test]] or [[Phillips–Perron test]].  If <math>\beta</math> is unknown, we must first estimate it. This is typically done by using [[ordinary least squares]] (by regressing <math>y_t</math> on <math>x_t</math> and an intercept). Then, we can run an ADF test on <math>u_t</math>. However, when <math>\beta</math> is estimated, the critical values of this ADF test are non-standard, and increase in absolute value as more regressors are included.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=MacKinnon |first=James G. |date=2010 |title=Critical values for cointegration tests |url=https://hdl.handle.net/10419/67744 |journal=Queen's Economics Department Working Paper |issue=1227 |via=EconStor}}</ref>

If the variables are found to be cointegrated, a second-stage regression is conducted. This is a regression of <math>\Delta y_t</math> on the lagged regressors, <math>\Delta x_t </math> and the lagged residuals from the first stage, <math>\hat{u}_{t-1}</math>. The second stage regression is given as:
<math>\Delta y_t = \Delta x_t b + \alpha u_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t</math>

If the variables are not cointegrated (if we cannot reject the null of no cointegration when testing <math>u_t</math>), then <math>\alpha=0</math> and we estimate a differences model: <math>\Delta y_t = \Delta x_t b + \varepsilon_t</math>

===Johansen test===
The [[Johansen test]] is a test for cointegration that allows for more than one cointegrating relationship, unlike the Engle–Granger method, but this test is subject to asymptotic properties, i.e. large samples. If the sample size is too small then the results will not be reliable and one should use Auto Regressive Distributed Lags (ARDL).<ref>{{cite web|last1=Giles|first1=David|title=ARDL Models - Part II - Bounds Tests|date=19 June 2013 |url=http://davegiles.blogspot.com/2013/06/ardl-models-part-ii-bounds-tests.html|access-date=4 August 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Pesaran|first1=M.H.|last2=Shin|first2=Y.|last3=Smith|first3=R.J.|title=Bounds testing approaches to the analysis of level relationships|journal=Journal of Applied Econometrics|date=2001|volume=16|issue=3|pages=289–326|doi=10.1002/jae.616|hdl=10983/25617|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

===Phillips–Ouliaris cointegration test===
[[Peter C. B. Phillips]] and [[Sam Ouliaris]] (1990) show that residual-based unit root tests applied to the estimated cointegrating residuals do not have the usual Dickey–Fuller distributions under the null hypothesis of no-cointegration.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=P. C. B. |last1=Phillips |first2=S. |last2=Ouliaris |title=Asymptotic Properties of Residual Based Tests for Cointegration |journal=[[Econometrica]] |volume=58 |issue=1 |year=1990 |pages=165–193 |jstor=2938339 |doi=10.2307/2938339 |url=http://cowles.yale.edu/sites/default/files/files/pub/d08/d0847-r.pdf |access-date=2019-12-14 |archive-date=2021-09-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210918174602/https://cowles.yale.edu/sites/default/files/files/pub/d08/d0847-r.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Because of the spurious regression phenomenon under the null hypothesis, the distribution of these tests have asymptotic distributions that depend on (1) the number of deterministic trend terms and (2) the number of variables with which co-integration is being tested. These distributions are known as Phillips–Ouliaris distributions and critical values have been tabulated. In finite samples, a superior alternative to the use of these asymptotic critical value is to generate critical values from simulations.

===Multicointegration===
In practice, cointegration is often used for two {{tmath|I(1)}} series, but it is more generally applicable and can be used for variables integrated of higher order (to detect correlated accelerations or other second-difference effects). '''Multicointegration''' extends the cointegration technique beyond two variables, and occasionally to variables integrated at different orders.

===Variable shifts in long time series===
Tests for cointegration assume that the cointegrating vector is constant during the period of study. In reality, it is possible that the long-run relationship between the underlying variables change (shifts in the cointegrating vector can occur). The reason for this might be technological progress, economic crises, changes in the people's preferences and behaviour accordingly, policy or regime alteration, and organizational or institutional developments. This is especially likely to be the case if the sample period is long. To take this issue into account, tests have been introduced for cointegration with one unknown [[structural break]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gregory |first1=Allan W. |last2=Hansen |first2=Bruce E. |year=1996 |title=Residual-based tests for cointegration in models with regime shifts |journal=Journal of Econometrics |volume=70 |issue=1 |pages=99–126 |doi=10.1016/0304-4076(69)41685-7 |url=https://www.econ.queensu.ca/sites/econ.queensu.ca/files/qed_wp_862.pdf }}</ref> and tests for cointegration with two unknown breaks are also available.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hatemi-J |first=A. |year=2008 |title=Tests for cointegration with two unknown regime shifts with an application to financial market integration |journal=[[Empirical Economics]] |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=497–505 |url=https://ideas.repec.org/a/spr/empeco/v35y2008i3p497-505.html |doi=10.1007/s00181-007-0175-9|s2cid=153437469 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Bayesian inference ===
Several [[Bayesian methods]] have been proposed to compute the posterior distribution of the number of cointegrating relationships and the cointegrating linear combinations.<ref>{{cite book |first1=G. |last1=Koop |first2=R. |last2=Strachan |first3=H.K. |last3=van Dijk |first4=M. |last4=Villani |editor-last1=Mills |editor-first1=T.C. |editor-last2=Patterson |editor-first2=K. |title=Handbook of Econometrics Vol.1 Econometric Theory |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |date=January 1, 2006 |pages=871–898 |chapter=Chapter 17: Bayesian Approaches to Cointegration |isbn=978-1-4039-4155-8 | url=https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/7750/}}</ref>
